extracted.intended_audience: students of literature and writers studying epigrams/humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short, witty epigrams in the style of Oscar Wilde — focusing on paradox, inversion, symmetry, and quotable phrasing. Useful for writers, humorists, and literature students aiming to emulate Wildean wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradox and Contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Built on paradox — the apparent contradiction that contains truth. Setup invokes a familiar form; punch substitutes a paradoxical term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'He atones for being occasionally somewhat over-dressed, by being always absolutely over-educated.' Use a recognizable setup then swap in a contradictory term that nevertheless reveals an insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallel grammatical structures and sound symmetry (rhythm, alliteration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the sentence grammatically and sonically so the epigram reads as a tight, mirrored unit; pay attention to rhythm and alliteration to enhance quotability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (subverting idioms/proverbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subverts a familiar idiom or proverb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'I can resist anything except temptation.' 'Work is the curse of the drinking classes.' Use a known saying or expectation and flip a key element to produce wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiar-Then-Surprising (invoke-and-frustrate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epigrams 'invoke a response and then frustrate it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the first half to set up a conventional reading, then frustrate that expectation with an unexpected twist — e.g., widow's 'hair has turned quite gold from grief.' The surprise should reframe the initial familiar cue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epigram vs. Aphorism (humor requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epigram: short, witty, often satirical or humorous. Aphorism: short, pithy, but not necessarily humorous. Wilde's aphorisms are typically also epigrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Wildean style prioritize wit/satire — aim for humor as well as pithiness when deciding whether a line functions as an epigram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Famous Wildean Pattern — Definition reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition reversal pattern: define a familiar word or concept by reversing expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'A cynic is a man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing.' Use definition-form to expose irony or contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Famous Wildean Pattern — Recommended vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern that recommends or endorses a vice as a witty position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I can resist everything except temptation.' Present a vice as irresistible or desirable to produce paradoxical humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Famous Wildean Pattern — Snobby observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations that express a snobby or ironic social viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Anyone who lives within their means suffers from a lack of imagination.' Use social-snobbery framing to invert values and reveal absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Famous Wildean Pattern — Self-deprecating brag
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-deprecating brag that simultaneously boasts and mocks oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I have nothing to declare except my genius.' Combine apparent humility with an undercutting boast to create comedic tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word economy and precision ('words were sacred')
rubrics_metrics.description: Words were sacred to Wilde; each word perfectly placed; each phrase linked to the next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor tight, precise language. Every word should earn its place; eliminate filler so the epigram is compact and quotable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subvert a familiar phrase, idiom, or sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it subvert a familiar phrase, idiom, or sentiment?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inversion or redefinition of known phrases to create the paradoxical effect central to Wildean wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language: tight, balanced, quotable
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the language tight, balanced, quotable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess rhythm, balance, and memorability; the line should be apt for quotation and re-use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied worldview or stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it imply a worldview or stance?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective epigrams often reveal (implicitly) an attitude toward people, society, or values; check whether the line suggests a consistent ironic standpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frustrate then resolve via wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it frustrate the reader's first reading and then resolve via wit?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The epigram should create an initial cognitive expectation and then overturn or reframe it so the reader experiences recognition/pleasure at the twist.
